newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican Q3 GDP seen above seven pct after new data.
newsitem.headline: Mexican Q3 GDP seen above seven pct after new data.

text.p: Mexico's third quarter gross domestic product growth could hit seven percent or higher because of stronger than expected industrial production data, economists said.

In the run-up to the release of the GDP report due on Thursday, economists are expecting a slight rally in Mexican financial markets as investors discount what could be more good news on the macroeconomic front.

In the most recent Reuters survey, the consensus GDP forecast was 6.47 percent. But after September industrial activity was reported on Monday up a resounding 14 percent, many analysts believe GDP forecasts may be conservative.
"That industrial production figure could mean economic growth in the third quarter could be seven percent or higher," said Sergio Martin, economist at ING Barings.
He said one of the reasons economists have been hesitant in bumping up their GDP forecasts is the Finance Ministry's well-publicized projection that economic growth for the year will be 3.7 percent.

But he said the government may be deliberately playing down the strength of the economy, partly because it prefers to be conservative, and also because its growth projection for 1997 is four percent, and that is easier to explain to the public if this year's GDP forecast is below that.

Hector Chavez, economist at Santander, raised his Q3 GDP projection to 7.4 percent after robust industrial activity in August. Following the September figure, "I have seen people increase their (GDP) forecasts to eight percent," he said.

Bolstering the GDP performance, he said, is a fairly healthy agricultural sector that appears to have withstood the drought early in the year. Agriculture accounts for only about 5 percent of GDP, however.

The bulk of the GDP report, accounting for about 70 percent, is the services sector, and he said this would enjoy some beneficial spillover from industrial activity, which makes up 25 percent of the GDP report.
But economists said any sense from the services sector data that the domestic economy was enjoying a rebound would still probably be premature.
"Even though the service numbers will appear strong...this largely derives from a strong industrial production performance," said Gray Newman of HSBC James Capel.
He said any hope that the Mexican consumer was on the rebound after his pumelling in the 1995 recession would be punctured by retail sales data due out on Friday.
Retail sales have remained mired at last year's recessionary level for most of this year.
